doc_summary: ARC Evals (posted by Beth Barnes) explains the redactions made to its autonomous-agent evaluation report because of the risk of advancing agent capabilities, and describes the human-supervision precautions used during agent runs. The post is mostly about publication and safety policy, with little on realism design, but it shows how they handle simulated humans, oversight, and situational awareness.

items.claim: In a setup, have the experimenter simulate the human's response according to a detailed task spec instead of letting the agent interact with a real non-consenting person, because this lets risky behaviors like phishing be investigated safely while the agent still gets realistic responses.
items.quote: When we wanted to investigate such activities (as in the targeted phishing task) the experimenter would instead simulate the response of the human as outlined in detail in the task spec.

items.claim: prefers capability evaluations that probe whether agents can notice and evade oversight over assuming supervision is sound, because an agent with enough situational awareness could take obfuscated actions that look benign to the overseer.
items.quote: One may wonder whether the oversight we used could be circumvented by a language agent with sufficient situational awareness, which could then potentially access the internet without oversight or limitations.

items.claim: Treats failure to find or exploit oversight vulnerabilities in evaluations as evidence of current incapability, but explicitly flags that this conclusion is time-limited and must be rechecked as capabilities improve.
items.quote: our evaluations strongly indicate these agents are not capable enough to discover and exploit these sorts of vulnerabilities or effectively hide their actions under supervision. As model capabilities improve this may change

items.claim: Distrusts relying on human supervision as a permanent safeguard, since evaluations themselves are what should signal when more careful handling of models is needed.
items.quote: we believe these kinds of capability evaluations are precisely what will inform us of the need to be more careful in the handling of models, and we will be closely watching for this.

items.claim: In a setup, keep a human approving every action in high-risk channels such as web browsing, but allow multi-step autoplay for routine low-risk steps, instead of uniform approval, because it balances safety with a more natural agent run.
items.quote: Experimenters would sometimes run several steps at a time without approving each one, especially when the agent was engaging in routine or low risk activities. Every action during web browsing is actively approved by a human overseer, with no autoplay.

items.claim: prefers redacting detailed transcripts and agent strength/weakness accounts over full publication when stakeholders lack consensus, because the capability-advancing risk is real, not merely hypothetical.
items.quote: In recognition of the absence of consensus, the relative lack of public dialogue, and the early-stage nature of our analysis, we have decided to err on the side of caution for the time being.

items.claim: Decides what to publish by weighing net risk, counterfactual timing (similar projects like LangChain arose independently), and stakeholder approval, while staying open to revising as analysis improves.
items.quote: Our best guess is also that a more complete publication would have been approved by a majority of relevant stakeholders, and is therefore not unduly unilateralist, though this could be established more carefully

items.claim: prefers keeping the option to release withheld material later, conditional on minimal risk or further analysis, over a permanent decision, because the early-stage analysis is uncertain.
items.quote: We may later make this material public if more detailed analysis gives us sufficient confidence that it would be justified.
